screens.title: Event Handling and Real-time DApp Updates
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why Ethereum events are central to building responsive decentralized applications. Events are emitted by smart contracts during transaction execution and stored as log entries in the transaction receipt. They let your DApp listen for meaningful actions — like a number changing or a token transferring — without repeatedly polling state. That reduces cost and latency while creating a live user experience. You will see how to declare events in Solidity, why the indexed keyword matters for efficient filtering, and how to subscribe with Web3. js to receive on('data'), on('changed') and on('error') callbacks. I will walk you through concrete code examples: declaring NumberChanged in SimpleStorage, emitting it when setNumber runs, and wiring a JavaScript listener that updates the UI and an event log in real time. We also cover practical safeguards: using fromBlock to avoid fetching huge histories, unsubscribing to prevent leaks, and preferring WebSocket providers for true push updates. By the end you will be able to implement event-driven UI updates and avoid common performance pitfalls.

Event Handling

Events are log entries emitted by contracts. They make DApps reactive and efficient by delivering on-chain signals to the UI.

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the hands-on and conceptual skills you'll gain. First, you will be able to explain what an Ethereum event is: a log entry produced by a contract during a transaction that helps DApps listen for specific actions without polling. Second, you will learn to subscribe to smart contract events using Web3. js so your application receives real-time notifications as soon as the blockchain records the event. Third, you'll learn how to filter events by indexed parameters or by block range to receive only relevant updates. Each objective is framed around real code examples, so you'll not only understand terms but see working Solidity declarations and JavaScript listeners. Expect to connect these skills in a final activity where you update a live display after a transaction triggers an event.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on operational practices you'll adopt when building production-grade DApps. You will learn to manage subscriptions carefully, unsubscribing when components unmount or when the user disconnects to prevent memory leaks and excess network traffic. You will also understand the trade-offs between HTTP polling and WebSocket providers: WebSockets are preferable for real-time push updates while HTTP often forces polling. Another objective is to detect and handle rare blockchain reorgs by using on('changed') callbacks and not treating a single event as irreversible until confirmations are adequate. Finally, you will learn to anticipate performance bottlenecks such as subscribing to allEvents without filters and how to lazy-load historical events when needed. These habits lead to more responsive, stable DApps and fewer surprises in user experience. Learning Objectives — Best Practices means operational skills: subscription lifecycle, provider choice, reorg handling, and performance-minded event queries.. In practical terms, operational skills and production safety. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: What is an Ethereum Event?
screens.narratorSegment: An Ethereum event is a structured log entry that a smart contract emits during transaction execution. When a contract executes an emit statement, the node stores the emitted record in the transaction receipt rather than in contract storage. That makes events efficient for signaling: they do not modify contract state but do create a searchable record that external clients can subscribe to. A practical example is an ERC-20 Transfer event. Instead of calling balanceOf repeatedly, a DApp subscribes to Transfer events to learn when tokens move. A common misconception is that events are part of storage; they are not. Events are logs and may be omitted by light clients unless the node indexes them. Use events for notifications and user-facing updates, but do not rely on them as canonical state—always query the contract when you need the authoritative value. For learning: think of events as push notifications from the blockchain. As a closing question: when would you still need to call a view function instead of depending solely on events? What is an Ethereum Event? means events are efficient signals stored in transaction receipts and indexed for searching; they are not a substitute for reading contract state.. In practical terms, events are on-chain logs that expose contract activity to dapps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › What is an Ethereum Event?
Definition

Event as a log entry

Events are emitted during transaction execution and stored in the receipt. They are searchable and efficient for notifying off-chain clients.

Analogy
Think of events as a printed receipt attached to a transaction: the official record for interested watchers, but not the contract's internal storage.
Concrete example
A Transfer event tells wallets when to update balances without asking the contract repeatedly.
Key Takeaway

Use events to build reactive UIs, but query contract state when you need authoritative values.

Quick notes
  • Events are cheaper than storage reads when used for notifications.
  • Nodes can index parameters marked indexed for fast lookup.
  • Event logs appear in transaction receipts and include block and tx metadata.
Common misconception
Do not assume logs are canonical state. If app logic depends on exact values, read the contract directly after an event.
Check your understanding
When an event is emitted and you receive it in the UI, what additional check might you perform before showing a final confirmation to the user?

screens.title: Declare and emit events in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Declaring events in Solidity is straightforward but has a few important details. You declare an event type with the event keyword and list parameters; you can mark up to three parameters as indexed so nodes can search logs by those values. In our SimpleStorage example the event declaration is event NumberChanged(address indexed setter, uint256 oldNumber, uint256 newNumber). Inside setNumber we capture the old value, update state, and then emit NumberChanged(msg. sender, _oldNumber, _newNumber). A concrete reason to store the old value first is to ensure the emitted log contains both the previous and the new state so listeners can compute deltas. A common mistake is emitting before updating state; order matters when listeners or off-chain indexing expect the contract to reflect the change at the time of the event. Also remember that events are not a substitute for persistent storage; they are a historical record. Practice writing a declaration, marking important fields indexed, and emitting after state change to make events useful and consistent. Declare and emit events in Solidity means capture old state, update storage, then emit the event so logs reflect the correct transition.. In practical terms, how to write event declarations and emit them safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Emit after state change
keyIdea.text: Capture old state, update storage, then emit the event so logs reflect the correct transition.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Declare & Emit
Solidity snippet
// SimpleStorage.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
    uint256 public myNumber;

    // Declare an event
    event NumberChanged(address indexed setter, uint256 oldNumber, uint256 newNumber);

    constructor(uint256 _initialNumber) {
        myNumber = _initialNumber;
    }

    function setNumber(uint256 _newNumber) public {
        uint256 _oldNumber = myNumber; // Store old value before changing
        myNumber = _newNumber;
        emit NumberChanged(msg.sender, _oldNumber, _newNumber); // Emit the event
    }
}
Notes: mark critical parameters as indexed so you can filter on them, and include both old and new values when helpful for the UI.
Explanation & example
Example scenario: a settings panel updates a number. By emitting the old and new values, an off-chain listener can show a human-friendly change log that includes who made the change and when.
Common mistake
Emitting before changing state can confuse indexers and off-chain logic; capture old state first, update storage, then emit.
Key Takeaway

Use indexed params for searchability and emit after state updates to keep logs consistent with contract state.

screens.title: Subscribe to events with Web3.js
screens.narratorSegment: Subscribing to contract events in Web3. js is a common pattern that uses the contract instance's events property. The typical flow is: ensure your contract object is initialized, call simpleStorageContract. events. EventName with options such as fromBlock and filter, and then attach handlers for on('data'), on('changed') and on('error'). A concrete example is subscribing to NumberChanged from the latest block: simpleStorageContract. events. NumberChanged({ fromBlock: 'latest' }). on('data', event => { /* update UI using event. returnValues */ }). The 'data' callback fires when a matching event is found, carrying returnValues, blockNumber and transactionHash. 'changed' fires if an event is removed due to a blockchain reorg, so use it to roll back UI changes or mark the event as non-final. The 'error' callback helps surface node or network issues. A common issue is failing to check that simpleStorageContract exists before subscribing — always guard and provide user feedback if the contract is not loaded. Finally, remember the subscription object lifecycle: track it and unsubscribe when appropriate to avoid duplicated listeners and memory growth. Subscribe to events with Web3.js means create, handle data/changed/error callbacks, and unsubscribe when the listener is no longer needed to preserve performance and correctness.. In practical terms, a walkthrough of the subscription pattern and callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Create, handle data/changed/error callbacks, and unsubscribe when the listener is no longer needed to preserve performance and correctness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Subscribe with Web3.js
Subscription snippet
// Assuming simpleStorageContract is initialized
simpleStorageContract.events.NumberChanged({
  fromBlock: 'latest' // only new events
})
.on('data', (event) => {
  // event.returnValues contains setter, oldNumber, newNumber
  const { setter, oldNumber, newNumber } = event.returnValues;
  console.log('NumberChanged', setter, oldNumber, newNumber);
  document.getElementById('displayNumber').textContent = newNumber;
})
.on('changed', (event) => {
  console.warn('Event removed by reorg', event);
})
.on('error', (error, receipt) => {
  console.error('Subscription error', error, receipt);
});
This pattern wires the data callback to update UI state immediately when new events arrive.
Explanation & checklist
  • Ensure contract instance is ready before subscribing.
  • Set fromBlock: 'latest' to avoid fetching history at startup unless needed.
  • Use filter for indexed params to reduce noise and network load.
  • Handle changed to detect reorgs and error to log provider issues.
Pro tip
If you need historical events for a timeline, fetch them separately with getPastEvents and present them lazily to avoid blocking initialization.

screens.title: Filtering and indexed parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Filtering events is crucial for efficiency. Solidity lets you mark up to three parameters as indexed. These indexed parameters are stored in the node's topic index, allowing queries that search by value. For example, NumberChanged declares address indexed setter; if your DApp only cares about changes from the current user, use filter: { setter: currentAccount } in the subscription options. This filtering happens at the node, so the client receives only matching events. A concrete example: subscribing to ListingCreated in an NFT marketplace with filter: { seller: specificSeller } delivers only that seller's listings. A common mistake is trying to filter on non-indexed fields — the node cannot filter those efficiently and will return broad results instead. Also, remember fromBlock: 'latest' versus a numeric block when you need past records. Use filters for indexed fields and design your event signatures so essential queryable attributes are indexed. Closing question: which fields of an event would you index to support your most frequent queries? Filtering and indexed parameters means mark parameters indexed when you expect to filter on them; otherwise filtering is expensive or impossible at the node level.. In practical terms, how to receive only the events you care about. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Filtering & Indexed Params
Indexed vs non-indexed
Indexed parameters are placed into topics and allow node-level filtering. Non-indexed parameters are part of the event data but cannot be efficiently filtered by the node.
Example signature
event NumberChanged(address indexed setter, uint256 oldNumber, uint256 newNumber);
Filter usage
simpleStorageContract.events.NumberChanged({ fromBlock: 'latest', filter: { setter: currentAccount } })
Two-panel comparison
Filtered
Client receives only matching events. Lower network and processing cost.
Unfiltered
Client must handle many events and perform client-side filtering, causing cost and latency.
Key Takeaway

Index the fields you will commonly filter on to let nodes return concise, relevant feeds to your DApp.

screens.title: Handling event callbacks and UI updates
screens.narratorSegment: Receiving an event in your listener is the moment to update application state and the user interface. The primary callback is on('data'), which provides an event object containing event. returnValues, blockNumber, and transactionHash. When you get a NumberChanged event, parse returnValues to extract setter, oldNumber, and newNumber. Update your displayed value and append a log entry so users see the history. A concrete example from the chapter shows updating displayNumber. textContent = newNumber and prepending a log entry that includes the block number. Be mindful of reorgs: on('changed') may fire if the event is removed; treat that as a signal to revert any optimistic UI change or mark the event as non-final. Error handling is also essential: on('error') catches subscription or provider issues, and you should show an unobtrusive error in the event log and retry logic if appropriate. A misconception is assuming events arrive only after a full confirmation; in many setups events are emitted when the transaction is mined in a block, and you may want to wait for additional confirmations before treating high-value changes as final. End by practicing: after you update the DOM from an event, how would you make the UI reflect finality?

keyIdea.title: From event to UI
keyIdea.text: Parse returnValues, update the display, log metadata, and handle changed and error callbacks to keep the interface correct and resilient.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Event Callbacks
Typical on('data') handler
.on('data', (event) => {
  const { setter, oldNumber, newNumber } = event.returnValues;
  const logEntry = `
NumberChanged by ${setter.substring(0,6)}... from ${oldNumber} to ${newNumber}. Block: ${event.blockNumber}
`;
  eventLog.innerHTML = logEntry + eventLog.innerHTML;
  document.getElementById('displayNumber').textContent = newNumber;
})
.on('changed', (event) => {
  // handle reorg: remove log entry or flag it as reverted
})
.on('error', (error) => {
  // show error in eventLog and consider retry
});
Update both the visible value and a persistent log so users can see history and context for the change.
UI considerations
  • Show a temporary indication if you wait for extra confirmations for finality.
  • Prepend new events so the most recent activity is visible at the top.
  • Gracefully show errors from on('error') and avoid blocking the main UI.
Common mistake

Treating a single mined event as final without considering confirmations can lead to showing incorrect information if a reorg happens.

screens.title: Managing fromBlock and historical events
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an appropriate fromBlock option prevents slow startups and heavy data transfers. The fromBlock parameter sets the starting point for the subscription or for past events queries. If you specify fromBlock: 'latest' you will only receive events emitted after your listener starts — this is perfect for live apps that do not need full history. If you need historical context, explicitly request a limited block range or use getPastEvents with a bounded fromBlock and toBlock and load results incrementally. A frequent beginner mistake is leaving fromBlock unspecified. Without it, Web3. js may attempt to retrieve all historical events from deployment to present, which can freeze or crash browsers for busy contracts. For example, for a wallet that only needs new transfers, use fromBlock: 'latest'. For an audit timeline, fetch past events page by page. Finally, always advise users when historical loading is in progress, and consider caching previously loaded history to reduce repeated network work. Follow these steps to make a live, event-driven UI and avoid common operational mistakes like missing unsubscribes or unspecified fromBlock.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why Ethereum events are central to building responsive decentralized applications. Events are emitted by smart contracts during transaction execution and stored as log entries in the transaction receipt. They let your DApp listen for meaningful actions — like a number changing or a token transferring — without repeatedly polling state. That reduces cost and latency while creating a live user experience. You will see how to declare events in Solidity, why the indexed keyword matters for efficient filtering, and how to subscribe with Web3. js to receive on('data'), on('changed') and on('error') callbacks. I will walk you through concrete code examples: declaring NumberChanged in SimpleStorage, emitting it when setNumber runs, and wiring a JavaScript listener that updates the UI and an event log in real time. We also cover practical safeguards: using fromBlock to avoid fetching huge histories, unsubscribing to prevent leaks, and preferring WebSocket providers for true push updates. By the end you will be able to implement event-driven UI updates and avoid common performance pitfalls.

These objectives guide the hands-on and conceptual skills you'll gain. First, you will be able to explain what an Ethereum event is: a log entry produced by a contract during a transaction that helps DApps listen for specific actions without polling. Second, you will learn to subscribe to smart contract events using Web3. js so your application receives real-time notifications as soon as the blockchain records the event. Third, you'll learn how to filter events by indexed parameters or by block range to receive only relevant updates. Fourth, you'll practice processing event. returnValues and using that data to update the DApp interface dynamically. Each objective is framed around real code examples, so you'll not only understand terms but see working Solidity declarations and JavaScript listeners. Expect to connect these skills in a final activity where you update a live display after a transaction triggers an event.

This second objectives slide focuses on operational practices you'll adopt when building production-grade DApps. You will learn to manage subscriptions carefully, unsubscribing when components unmount or when the user disconnects to prevent memory leaks and excess network traffic. You will also understand the trade-offs between HTTP polling and WebSocket providers: WebSockets are preferable for real-time push updates while HTTP often forces polling. Another objective is to detect and handle rare blockchain reorgs by using on('changed') callbacks and not treating a single event as irreversible until confirmations are adequate. Finally, you will learn to anticipate performance bottlenecks such as subscribing to allEvents without filters and how to lazy-load historical events when needed. These habits lead to more responsive, stable DApps and fewer surprises in user experience. An Ethereum event is a structured log entry that a smart contract emits during transaction execution. When a contract executes an emit statement, the node stores the emitted record in the transaction receipt rather than in contract storage. That makes events efficient for signaling: they do not modify contract state but do create a searchable record that external clients can subscribe to. A practical example is an ERC-20 Transfer event. Instead of calling balanceOf repeatedly, a DApp subscribes to Transfer events to learn when tokens move. A common misconception is that events are part of storage; they are not. Events are logs and may be omitted by light clients unless the node indexes them. Use events for notifications and user-facing updates, but do not rely on them as canonical state—always query the contract when you need the authoritative value.
